items.followUp: A solution contains 8 g of salt in 200 cm³ of solution. Calculate its percentage mass/volume concentration.

rubric.why: Identifies the meaning of percentage mass/volume.
rubric.description: States the mass of solute present in 100 cm³ of solution.
rubric.how: Award for a correct definition relating grams of solute to 100 cm³ of solution.

rubric.why: Shows the definition applied in an example.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example, such as 5 g of solute in 100 cm³ of solution (5% m/v).
rubric.how: Award for a correct example with the amount of solute and solution volume.

modelAnswer: Percentage mass/volume is the mass of solute, in grams, dissolved in 100 cm³ of solution.
For example, a solution containing 5 g of salt in 100 cm³ of solution has a concentration of 5% mass/volume.

items.followUp: Name four metals that are less reactive than potassium but more reactive than copper.

rubric.why: Assesses knowledge of the names of reactive metals.
rubric.description: Names any four very reactive metals.
rubric.how: Award 0.5 mark for each correct metal, up to four. Accept potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc or iron.

modelAnswer: Four very reactive metals are potassium, sodium, calcium and magnesium.

items.followUp: What is a transition metal? Name one transition metal and give one characteristic property.

rubric.why: Assesses the defining electronic feature of transition metals.
rubric.description: Defines transition metals as elements with an incompletely filled d-subshell in their atoms or ions.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the partially filled or incomplete d-subshell.

rubric.why: Assesses an appropriate example.
rubric.description: Gives an example of a transition metal.
rubric.how: Award for any valid example, such as iron or copper.

modelAnswer: Transition metals are elements whose atoms or ions have a partially filled d-subshell.
Iron (Fe) is an example.

items.followUp: State how metallic character changes down a group and across a period.

rubric.why: Assesses the periodic trend across a period.
rubric.description: States that non-metallic character increases from left to right across a period.
rubric.how: Award for the correct direction across a period.

rubric.why: Assesses the periodic trend down a group.
rubric.description: States that non-metallic character decreases down a group.
rubric.how: Award for the correct direction down a group.

modelAnswer: Across a period, non-metallic character increases from left to right.
Down a group, non-metallic character decreases.

items.followUp: Write the equation for the reaction of methane with chlorine in diffused sunlight and name the type of reaction.

rubric.why: Assesses the products of methane chlorination.
rubric.description: Identifies chloromethane and hydrogen chloride as the products.
rubric.how: Award for both products or a correct balanced equation.

rubric.why: Assesses the reaction conditions and equation.
rubric.description: Shows that chlorine substitutes for one hydrogen in methane in diffused sunlight.
rubric.how: Award for the correct condition and substitution equation.

modelAnswer: In diffused sunlight, chlorine substitutes for one hydrogen atom in methane.
CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl
The products are chloromethane and hydrogen chloride.

items.followUp: State two limitations of Rutherford’s atomic model and the questions these raised about atomic structure.

rubric.why: Assesses the stability problem in Rutherford’s model.
rubric.description: Explains that a revolving electron should radiate energy, lose energy and eventually spiral into the nucleus, so the model could not explain atomic stability.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the predicted loss of energy and 1 mark for the resulting instability or spiral into the nucleus.

rubric.why: Assesses the question raised by the stability defect.
rubric.description: States the question of why electrons do not fall into the nucleus and how the atom remains stable.
rubric.how: Award for a clear stability question.

rubric.why: Assesses another limitation of Rutherford’s model.
rubric.description: States that the model could not explain the line spectrum of atoms, such as hydrogen.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the unexplained atomic line spectrum.

rubric.why: Assesses the questions raised about electron arrangement.
rubric.description: Raises the question of how electrons are arranged or distributed around the nucleus, including whether they occupy specific orbits or energy levels.
rubric.how: Award for a relevant question about electron arrangement or orbits.

modelAnswer: Rutherford’s model could not explain the stability of the atom: a revolving electron should radiate energy, lose energy and spiral into the nucleus.
This raised the question: Why do electrons not lose energy and fall into the nucleus? How does an atom remain stable?
The model could not explain the line spectrum of atoms.
This raised the question of how electrons are arranged around the nucleus and whether they occupy specific orbits or energy levels.

items.followUp: Define empirical formula and give the empirical formula of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, and magnesium chloride, MgCl₂.

rubric.why: Assesses the definition and its application to formula units.
rubric.description: Defines empirical formula as the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound, or ions in an ionic compound.
rubric.how: Award for the simplest whole-number ratio and for correctly including atoms/ions.

rubric.why: Assesses the empirical formula of a covalent compound.
rubric.description: Explains that the empirical formula gives the simplest ratio and need not show the actual molecular number of atoms; gives glucose as CH₂O.
rubric.how: Award for CH₂O from glucose, or an equivalent correct covalent example and explanation.

rubric.why: Assesses the formula-unit ratio in an ionic compound.
rubric.description: Explains that an ionic empirical formula shows the simplest ratio of ions; gives magnesium chloride as MgCl₂.
rubric.how: Award for the correct ionic ratio or example.

modelAnswer: An empirical formula represents the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound; for an ionic compound, it represents the simplest ratio of ions in its formula unit.
For a covalent compound, the empirical formula may differ from the molecular formula. For example, glucose has molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆ and empirical formula CH₂O.
For an ionic compound, the formula gives the simplest ratio of ions. For example, MgCl₂ represents a 1:2 ratio of magnesium ions to chloride ions.

items.followUp: Explain why metals conduct electricity and define the metallic bond.

rubric.why: Assesses the positive particles in a metal lattice.
rubric.description: States that metal atoms form positive ions or positive metal kernels.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the positive metal particles.

rubric.why: Assesses the mobile electrons in metallic bonding.
rubric.description: States that valence electrons become delocalised or mobile throughout the metal.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the delocalised/mobile electrons.

rubric.why: Assesses the definition and nature of the bond.
rubric.description: Defines a metallic bond as the electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons, and explains that this attraction holds the metal together.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the attraction between the two kinds of particles and 1 mark for stating that it holds the metal lattice together.

rubric.why: Assesses a consequence of the metallic-bond model.
rubric.description: Links freely moving electrons with electrical conductivity.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that mobile electrons carry charge through the metal.

modelAnswer: Metallic bonding occurs in a metal lattice of positive metal ions surrounded by delocalised valence electrons.
A metallic bond is the electrostatic force of attraction between the positive metal ions and the sea of delocalised electrons.
This attraction holds the metal lattice together.
The electrons can move freely through the lattice, so metals conduct electricity.
